claims.text: A computational free-energy sampling framework can identify an optimal processing window for RHEA/Cu composite synthesis.
The identified processing window will overcome the high positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu.
Overcoming the positive heat of mixing will enable a large-scale, uniform reaction.
The proposed method will produce a stable RHEA/Cu composite microstructure.
RHEA powders and Cu particles in the precursor are initially segregated because of unfavorable mixing enthalpies.
Free-energy sampling can determine precise high-temperature, pressure, and reaction-time conditions for reactive synthesis.
Controlled high temperature, pressure, and reaction time can accelerate reaction kinetics during RHEA/Cu processing.
Advanced sintering or reactive blending under controlled conditions can limit phase segregation in RHEA/Cu composites.
High-temperature and high-pressure processing can drive microstructural and interfacial evolution.
Refinement of refractory–Cu phase boundaries promotes uniform intermixing and diffusion.
Sampling the free-energy landscape can identify processing parameters that reduce thermodynamic barriers associated with positive mixing enthalpy.
Reducing these thermodynamic barriers enhances atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility facilitates uniform reactive synthesis.
The proposed process will produce a homogeneous microstructure with minimized segregation at refractory-element/Cu interfaces.
A homogeneous, stable RHEA/Cu microstructure will enhance mechanical strength.
A homogeneous, stable RHEA/Cu microstructure will enhance irradiation resistance.
Conventional arc melting and standard additive manufacturing do not account for the thermodynamic barriers in RHEA/Cu mixing.
Conventional processing of RHEA/Cu composites often produces non-uniform phases and interfacial instabilities.
The approach is effective only if the sampled free-energy landscape accurately represents reaction kinetics at processing scale.
Extreme processing deviations or unexpected interfacial reactions could limit the efficacy of the approach.
